etymology: From Latin justificare, to make or declare righteous, from justus (righteous) and facere (to make). Webster 1828: pronounced or regarded as just; absolved from guilt. In Scripture the word is forensic — a verdict pronounced by the Judge, not a quality infused into the defendant.
biblical_def: Justified is the Bible’s word for the sinner’s standing declared righteous before God. It is a courtroom word, not a hospital word: the Judge does not repair the guilty man and then acquit him, He acquits him on the ground of another’s righteousness imputed. Paul states the ground and the instrument in one breath: Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:24). Freely excludes price paid by the sinner; by his grace excludes merit; through the redemption names the price that was in fact paid, and it was paid by Christ. The instrument by which the sinner receives this verdict is faith alone: Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 5:1). Peace is not a feeling produced by the verdict but the state created by it — the war is over because the charge is gone. The verdict is unbreakable because it is one link in a chain God Himself forged: whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified (Romans 8:30). Not one justified man falls out between the second link and the third. And the verdict falls on the unlikeliest: after cataloguing fornicators, idolaters, thieves and drunkards, Paul writes, And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 6:11).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines JUSTIFIED as pronounced or regarded as just; absolved from guilt or the charge of sin; freed by pardon; vindicated. Webster notes the theological sense explicitly: in the scriptural sense, freed from the penalty of sin and accepted as righteous on account of the merits of Christ.
webster_full: JUSTIFIED, pp. — Proved or shown to be just; vindicated; cleared from blame.
Absolved from guilt; freed by pardon from the penalty due to sin.
In theology, accounted or accepted as righteous before God, not on the ground of personal obedience, but on account of the merits and righteousness of Christ received by faith.
Distinguished from sanctified: the one is a change of state before the law, the other a change of nature within the man.
From Latin justus, just, and facio, to make — the root also of justice, justify, and injustice.
scriptures: Romans 3:24
Being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus:
Romans 5:1
Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ:
Romans 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
1 Corinthians 6:11
And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.
Titus 3:7
That being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.
corruption_summary: The Council of Trent anathematized the doctrine that justification is a declared verdict received by faith alone, and modern reconstructions of Paul have revived the substance of that denial by making justification a statement about who belongs to the covenant community rather than how a guilty man is acquitted.
corruption_paragraphs: Rome’s error is precise and it has never been withdrawn. Trent’s sixth session defined justification as a translation from a state of sin to a state of grace by means of infused righteousness, increased by good works and lost by mortal sin, and its canons pronounced anathema on anyone teaching that the sinner is justified by faith alone or that the righteousness by which he is justified is the righteousness of Christ imputed. That is not a difference of emphasis with the Reformation; it is the denial of Romans 3:24 and Romans 5:1 at the point where they are clearest. If justification is a process rather than a verdict, no man can have peace with God in this life, because no man knows whether the process is complete — which is exactly the pastoral misery the Reformation delivered the church from.

The newer corruption wears Protestant clothes. Recent reconstructions of Paul relocate justification from the courtroom to the question of covenant membership: the doctrine is said to answer not how can a guilty man stand before God but who counts as belonging to the people of God, and the imputation of Christ’s active obedience is set aside as a category the apostle never used. But Romans 8:30 chains justification to predestination on one side and glorification on the other — it is an act of God upon an individual sinner in eternity’s ordering, not a social marker. And 1 Corinthians 6:11 names fornicators, idolaters and drunkards as the men justified, which is a statement about guilt removed, not about a boundary line redrawn.
roots_summary: Greek dikaioo (G1344), to declare righteous, to acquit; dikaiosis (G1347), the act of acquittal; dikaiosune (G1343), righteousness; Hebrew tsadaq (H6663), to be just, to be declared in the right.
roots_lines: Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, to pronounce just; used forensically of a judge’s verdict (Romans 3:24, 5:1, 8:30).
Greek dikaiosis (G1347) — the act of acquittal; raised again for our justification (Romans 4:25).
Greek dikaiosune (G1343) — righteousness; the standing conferred, imputed to the believer (Romans 4:6).
Hebrew tsadaq (H6663) — to be right, to be declared in the right; the judge who justifieth the wicked is an abomination (Proverbs 17:15) apart from a satisfaction.
Greek logizomai (G3049) — to reckon, to impute; the accounting term behind counted unto him for righteousness (Romans 4:3).
usage: Being justified freely by his grace (Romans 3:24) — the ground of the verdict is grace, not the sinner’s improvement.
Justified by faith, we have peace with God (Romans 5:1) — the verdict creates the peace, not the reverse.
Whom he justified, them he also glorified (Romans 8:30) — the chain from which no justified man is lost.

etymology: From Latin sanctificare, to make holy, from sanctus (holy) and facere (to make). Webster 1828: made holy; consecrated; set apart to a sacred use. Scripture carries both senses — the definitive setting-apart accomplished once at the cross, and the progressive making-holy wrought daily by the Spirit.
biblical_def: Sanctified in Scripture is first a completed fact and only then a continuing work, and reversing that order has wrecked more assurance than almost any other mistake. The completed fact: By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Hebrews 10:10). The verb is past, the offering is once for all, and the sanctifying is accomplished by the will of God and the body of Christ — not by the believer’s progress. So Paul can address quarrelling, litigious Corinthians as men already sanctified: ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 6:11), and Luke can describe the whole company of the saved simply as them which are sanctified (Acts 20:32). The Lord Himself is the ground: And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth (John 17:19) — Christ consecrating Himself to the altar so that His people might be consecrated in Him. The continuing work follows from the fact and never founds it: And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless (1 Thessalonians 5:23). The whole man is the object; God is the agent; the prayer is a prayer because the work is His.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines SANCTIFIED as made holy; consecrated; set apart for sacred services; freed from sin; purified. Webster distinguishes the ceremonial sense (set apart to a holy use) from the moral sense (cleansed from the pollution of sin and made holy in heart).
webster_full: SANCTIFIED, pp. — Made holy; consecrated; set apart for a sacred purpose or use.
Freed from the power and pollution of sin; purified in heart; made holy in disposition and conduct.
Affected by holy influences; as, an affliction sanctified to the soul’s profit.
In the ceremonial sense, separated from a common to a sacred use, as the vessels of the tabernacle or the seventh day.
From Latin sanctus, holy, and facio, to make — the root also of saint, sanctuary, and sanction.
scriptures: Hebrews 10:10
By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.
John 17:19
And for their sakes I sanctify myself, that they also might be sanctified through the truth.
1 Corinthians 6:11
And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified in the name of the Lord Jesus, and by the Spirit of our God.
1 Thessalonians 5:23
And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Acts 20:32
And now, brethren, I commend you to God, and to the word of his grace, which is able to build you up, and to give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified.
corruption_summary: Two opposite errors attack the word: perfectionism, which claims the progressive work can be finished in this life by a second crisis of grace, and antinomian passivity, which treats the definitive fact as excusing the daily fight the New Testament everywhere commands.
corruption_paragraphs: Perfectionism — whether in its Wesleyan entire-sanctification form, the nineteenth-century Higher Life and Keswick teaching of a second blessing, or the modern deliverance ministries that promise a decisive break from indwelling sin — reads 1 Thessalonians 5:23 as a promise of attainable sinlessness and forgets that Paul is praying, and that he ends the same letter still commending the Thessalonians to God’s faithfulness to do it. Romans 7 and Galatians 5:17 describe the settled condition of the regenerate man: the flesh warring against the Spirit so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. A doctrine that promises the end of that war before glory produces either pretence or despair, and church history shows it has produced both.

The opposite error takes Hebrews 10:10 as the whole account and treats the daily mortification of sin as optional refinement. But the same epistle that says we are sanctified also says follow… holiness, without which no man shall see the Lord (Hebrews 12:14), and John 17:19 grounds the ongoing work in the truth — meaning ordinary means, the Word read and preached, applied by the Spirit over years. Owen’s rule stands: be killing sin or it will be killing you. The definitive fact is the ground of the fight, never a substitute for it, and 1 Corinthians 6:11 says such were some of you, past tense, about behaviour Paul then spends four chapters correcting.
roots_summary: Greek hagiazo (G37), to set apart as holy, to consecrate; hagiasmos (G38), sanctification; hagios (G40), holy, saint; Hebrew qadash (H6942), to be set apart, to consecrate.
roots_lines: Greek hagiazo (G37) — to make holy, to set apart to God; used of the definitive act (Hebrews 10:10) and of Christ consecrating Himself (John 17:19).
Greek hagiasmos (G38) — sanctification, the state and the process; this is the will of God, even your sanctification (1 Thessalonians 4:3).
Greek hagios (G40) — holy; in the plural the ordinary New Testament word for believers, the saints.
Hebrew qadash (H6942) — to be set apart, consecrated; used of the seventh day, the tabernacle vessels, and the firstborn.
Hebrew qodesh (H6944) — holiness, a holy thing; the root behind the holy place and the most holy.
usage: Sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all (Hebrews 10:10) — the definitive act, already complete.
Ye are sanctified… in the name of the Lord Jesus (1 Corinthians 6:11) — said to the most disorderly church in the New Testament.
The very God of peace sanctify you wholly (1 Thessalonians 5:23) — the progressive work, asked of God because it is God’s to give.

etymology: From Greek baptizo, to dip, to immerse, to plunge; the intensive of bapto, to dip. Webster 1828: administered the sacrament of baptism to; christened. The Greek word was ordinary before it was ecclesiastical — used of dyeing cloth by dipping and of a ship sunk in the sea.
biblical_def: Baptized describes what was done to every believer in the book of Acts, and the New Testament never pictures an unbaptized Christian. The order is fixed: the word is heard, the word is received, and the receivers are baptized. Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls (Acts 2:41). Gladly receiving precedes the water; nothing in the sentence permits reversal. The Lord Himself submitted to it as the opening act of His public ministry: And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water (Matthew 3:16) — out of the water, which is the plain description of a man who had been in it. Paul makes the mode the picture of the meaning: Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? (Romans 6:3). Burial and rising are the figure, and immersion is the only mode that shows it. And the outward act signifies an inward and Spirit-wrought union: For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free (1 Corinthians 12:13). The sign does not create the union; it declares it, and the church receives the one baptized as a member of the body Christ purchased.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BAPTIZED as having received the ordinance of baptism; christened. Webster’s entry for the verb notes that the Greek word signifies to dip or immerse, and that the practice of the primitive church was immersion, sprinkling and pouring having been introduced later.
webster_full: BAPTIZED, pp. — Having received the ordinance of baptism; initiated by water into the visible church.
The Greek baptizo signifies properly to dip, to plunge, to immerse; and this was the practice of the primitive church.
Figuratively, overwhelmed or immersed in suffering; as, the baptism of blood which Christ endured.
Applied also to the descent of the Holy Spirit upon the church, called the baptism of the Holy Ghost.
From Greek bapto, to dip — the root also of baptism, Baptist, and baptistery.
scriptures: Acts 2:41
Then they that gladly received his word were baptized: and the same day there were added unto them about three thousand souls.
Matthew 3:16
And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him:
Romans 6:3
Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death?
1 Corinthians 12:13
For by one Spirit are we all baptized into one body, whether we be Jews or Gentiles, whether we be bond or free; and have been all made to drink into one Spirit.
corruption_summary: Baptismal regeneration makes the water do what only the Spirit does, and paedobaptism reverses the New Testament order by administering the sign to those who have not yet gladly received the word.
corruption_paragraphs: Baptismal regeneration — held by Rome, by the Eastern churches, and in varying strength by Lutheran and Anglican sacramental theology — teaches that the water conveys the new birth rather than signifying it. Acts 2:41 forbids this at the level of grammar: they gladly received the word, and then were baptized. Simon Magus in Acts 8 was baptized and remained in the gall of bitterness, and in the bond of iniquity, which settles the question by counter-example. The sign seals a reality already given; a seal on an empty deed conveys nothing, and the pastoral damage of teaching otherwise is a congregation of the baptized-and-unconverted who have been told the decisive thing already happened to them in infancy.

Paedobaptism is the graver error among Reformed brethren precisely because so much else in their theology is sound, and the dictionary names it as error rather than difference. The argument runs from circumcision as the covenant sign given to infants, but the New Covenant is expressly the covenant in which they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest (Hebrews 8:11) — a covenant without an unregenerate membership. Every baptism recorded in Acts follows a credible profession, and Romans 6:3 defines the act as a burial into Christ’s death, which cannot be predicated of an infant who has not died with Him. The 1689 Confession states the Baptist position plainly and the dictionary holds it: the subjects are those who actually profess repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, and the mode is immersion.
roots_summary: Greek baptizo (G907), to immerse, to submerge; baptisma (G908), the act of immersion; bapto (G911), to dip; Hebrew tabal (H2881), to dip, used of Naaman dipping seven times in Jordan.
roots_lines: Greek baptizo (G907) — to dip repeatedly, to immerge, to submerge; the ordinary word for sinking a vessel or dyeing cloth.
Greek baptisma (G908) — the ordinance itself; the New Testament coined this noun for the Christian rite.
Greek bapto (G911) — the simple verb, to dip; dip the tip of his finger in water (Luke 16:24).
Hebrew tabal (H2881) — to dip; Naaman dipped himself seven times in Jordan (2 Kings 5:14), the Old Testament picture of cleansing by immersion.
Greek louo (G3068) and nipto (G3538) — to wash the whole body and to wash a part; the New Testament keeps these distinct from baptizo.
usage: They that gladly received his word were baptized (Acts 2:41) — the fixed New Testament order of profession before water.
Went up straightway out of the water (Matthew 3:16) — the Lord’s own baptism describing the mode.
Baptized into his death (Romans 6:3) — the meaning the mode was chosen to picture.

etymology: From Latin creare, to bring forth, to produce, to make. Webster 1828: formed from nothing; caused to exist. The Hebrew bara that stands behind the word in Genesis is used in the Old Testament only with God as its subject — no creature ever bara.
biblical_def: Created is the fourth word of the Bible and it settles everything that follows: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Genesis 1:1). There is no pre-existing material, no rival, no struggle, and no process; there is God, and then there is a universe because He spoke. The Hebrew verb bara takes only God as its subject throughout the Old Testament, which is Scripture’s own way of marking the act as incommunicable. The same verb governs the making of man, three times in one verse for emphasis: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them (Genesis 1:27). Image and sex are given in the same breath and by the same act, so that the two sexes are not a later social arrangement but the form in which the image was issued. The New Testament names the Agent: For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible… all things were created by him, and for him (Colossians 1:16). The Son is not the first creature but the Creator, and the thrones and dominions men fear are items on His inventory. And the same word describes the second creation: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works (Ephesians 2:10) — the new birth is a creative act, not a repair.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CREATED as formed from nothing; caused to exist; produced; brought into being. Webster distinguishes the strict sense — to cause to exist without pre-existing materials, an act proper to God alone — from the looser sense of shaping or constituting from what already exists.
webster_full: CREATED, pp. — Formed from nothing; caused to exist; brought into being by the divine power.
In the strict sense, to produce without the aid of pre-existing materials — an act of omnipotence proper to God alone.
In a secondary sense, to make, form, or shape out of existing materials; as, God created man of the dust of the ground.
Figuratively, to constitute or appoint; as, to create a peer; and in Scripture, to renew or regenerate the heart.
From Latin creo, creare — the root also of creature, creation, and recreate.
scriptures: Genesis 1:1
In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Genesis 1:27
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.
Colossians 1:16

For by him were all things created, that are in heaven, and that are in earth, visible and invisible, whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers: all things were created by him, and for him:
Ephesians 2:10
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
corruption_summary: Theistic evolution reduces created to a word for a process God supervised rather than an act He performed, and the modern denial that sex is given in the creative act sets Genesis 1:27 aside at exactly the point where it is most explicit.
corruption_paragraphs: Theistic evolution keeps the word and empties it. If God created man by superintending a chain of descent from earlier creatures, then Adam is not the first man but a selected one, death precedes sin rather than entering by it, and Romans 5:12 loses the historical Adam on whom the whole argument of imputation depends. Genesis 1:1 uses bara of an absolute beginning and Genesis 1:27 uses it again of man; Exodus 20:11 grounds the fourth commandment in six days of making. The dictionary’s position is six literal days and a historical Adam formed from the dust, and it holds that the framework and day-age readings were adopted to accommodate a scientific consensus rather than derived from the text.

The second corruption is the modern separation of sex from the creative act. Genesis 1:27 issues the image and the sexed body together — male and female created he them — and the Lord Jesus grounded the whole doctrine of marriage on that verse: he which made them at the beginning made them male and female (Matthew 19:4). To say that a person’s sex was assigned at birth rather than given in creation is to treat the body as an accident laid over an autonomous inner self, which is not a new idea but the old Gnostic contempt for the flesh wearing therapeutic language. The imago Dei in every such person is affirmed without qualification; the claim that the body may be corrected to match the mind is named as a corruption of Genesis 1:27.
roots_summary: Hebrew bara (H1254), to create, with God alone as subject; asah (H6213), to make or fashion; yatsar (H3335), to form as a potter; Greek ktizo (G2936), to create, to found.
roots_lines: Hebrew bara (H1254) — to create; in the qal it never takes a human subject, marking the act as God’s alone (Genesis 1:1, 1:27; Isaiah 45:7).
Hebrew asah (H6213) — to make, do, fashion; used alongside bara of the six days (Genesis 1:31; Exodus 20:11).
Hebrew yatsar (H3335) — to form, as a potter shapes clay; the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground (Genesis 2:7).
Greek ktizo (G2936) — to create, to found; all things were created by him (Colossians 1:16).
Greek ktisis (G2937) — the creation, the thing created; if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature (2 Corinthians 5:17).
usage: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth (Genesis 1:1) — creation out of nothing, by the word of God.
Male and female created he them (Genesis 1:27) — the image and the sexed body given in one act.
Created in Christ Jesus unto good works (Ephesians 2:10) — regeneration as a second creative act.

etymology: From Latin crucifigere, to fasten to a cross, from crux (cross) and figere (to fix). Webster 1828: nailed to a cross; put to death on a cross; mortified or subdued, as the flesh. The Romans reserved the punishment for slaves and rebels; Cicero called it the most cruel and shameful of penalties.
biblical_def: Crucified names both the historical death of Christ and the believer’s union with that death, and the New Testament will not let the two be separated. Paul reduced his entire preaching programme to the first: For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2). Not Christ in general but Christ under the curse, hanging on a tree, bearing wrath — that is the message, and Paul deliberately chose it over the rhetorical wisdom Corinth prized. But the same apostle speaks of himself in the same tense: I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me (Galatians 2:20). The believer did not merely benefit from the cross; he was on it in his Substitute, and the life he now lives is a life lent to a dead man. Romans states the consequence for indwelling sin: our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin (Romans 6:6). Crucifixion was slow, and so is mortification, but the verdict is already passed. Finally the cross severs the believer from the world in both directions: the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world (Galatians 6:14) — each is a corpse to the other, and Paul will glory in nothing else.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CRUCIFIED as nailed to a cross; put to death on a cross; and, in the figurative scriptural sense, mortified, subdued, or destroyed as to the power of sin and the affections of the flesh.
webster_full: CRUCIFIED, pp. — Nailed to a cross; put to death by nailing the hands and feet to a cross.
Subdued; mortified; destroyed as to its dominion; as, the flesh with its affections and lusts.
Made dead to; separated by the cross from; as, the world is crucified to the believer.
In the passive scriptural sense, having died with Christ so that the old man no longer reigns.
From Latin crux, a cross, and figo, to fix — the root also of cross, crucial, and excruciating.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 2:2
For I determined not to know any thing among you, save Jesus Christ, and him crucified.
Galatians 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
Romans 6:6
Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.
Galatians 6:14
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
corruption_summary: The moral-influence and moral-example theories of the atonement keep the crucifixion and delete its substance, and the modern complaint that penal substitution amounts to divine child abuse attacks the Trinity as much as the atonement.
corruption_paragraphs: Abelard’s moral-influence theory, revived in nineteenth-century liberalism and standard in progressive evangelical writing today, holds that the cross demonstrates God’s love and thereby moves men to repent, but effects no propitiation. The New Testament forecloses this. If Christ crucified merely displays love, then 1 Corinthians 2:2 is a strange thing to build a ministry on, Galatians 3:13 has no meaning when it says He was made a curse for us, and 1 John 2:2 is unintelligible when it calls Him the propitiation for our sins. A display of love that averts no wrath is not love toward men in danger; it is theatre. The cross demonstrates love precisely because it accomplishes substitution — Romans 5:8 makes the demonstration depend on the death being for sinners.

The charge that penal substitution is cosmic or divine child abuse assumes an unwilling victim and two separate wills. Both assumptions are false. The Son says I lay down my life, that I might take it again. No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself (John 10:17-18), and the Father and the Son are one God of one undivided will, so the covenant of redemption is not a transaction between two parties but the eternal purpose of one God executed by the Persons in their proper offices. Where the objection succeeds is against a caricature in which an angry Father is placated by a reluctant third party; it has no purchase on Chalcedonian Christology, and the objection is generally advanced by writers who have already abandoned the classical doctrine of God.
roots_summary: Greek stauroo (G4717), to crucify, to impale on a stake; sustauroo (G4957), to crucify together with; stauros (G4716), a cross; Hebrew talah (H8518), to hang, as of one hanged on a tree under the curse.
roots_lines: Greek stauroo (G4717) — to fasten to a stake or cross; the ordinary verb for the Roman execution (1 Corinthians 2:2).
Greek sustauroo (G4957) — to crucify together with; used of the two thieves and of the believer’s union with Christ (Romans 6:6; Galatians 2:20).
Greek stauros (G4716) — a cross, an upright stake; by metonymy the whole doctrine of the atonement (Galatians 6:14).
Hebrew talah (H8518) — to hang; he that is hanged is accursed of God (Deuteronomy 21:23), the verse Paul cites in Galatians 3:13.
Greek anastauroo (G388) — to crucify afresh; the apostates of Hebrews 6:6 crucify to themselves the Son of God afresh.
usage: Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Corinthians 2:2) — the deliberate narrowing of apostolic preaching.
I am crucified with Christ (Galatians 2:20) — the believer’s union with the death he did not die.
The world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world (Galatians 6:14) — a double severance, both ways.

etymology: From Latin convertere, to turn about, to turn round, from con (wholly) and vertere (to turn). Webster 1828: changed or turned from one state to another; turned from one religion or party to another; turned from sin to holiness. The core image is a man walking one way who turns and walks the other.
biblical_def: Converted in Scripture means turned — a whole man wheeling about, away from sin and toward God. It is not a synonym for regeneration but its visible face: regeneration is the new life given, conversion is the turning that new life produces. The Lord makes it non-negotiable: Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 18:3). The disciples were disputing about greatness; the answer was that they must be turned around before the question could even be asked properly. Peter preaches it as command paired with promise: Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord (Acts 3:19). Repentance and conversion stand together, and the blotting out of sins follows. David sees the fruit of his own restoration in the conversion of others: Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee (Psalm 51:13) — the pardoned man becomes the teacher, and the harvest is other men turned. And the Lord uses the word of Peter’s recovery after denial: when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren (Luke 22:32), which shows the term can cover a decisive turning back within the life of a true believer, not conversion twice over but restoration after grievous fall.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines CONVERTED as changed or turned from one substance, state, opinion, or religion to another; and in the scriptural and evangelical sense, turned from sin to God, from the love of sin to the love of holiness, by the operation of divine grace upon the heart.
webster_full: CONVERTED, pp. — Changed or turned from one state, form, or use to another.
Turned from one religion, party, or opinion to another; as, a heathen converted to Christianity.
In theology, turned from sin to God; changed in heart and life by the renewing influence of the Holy Spirit.
Applied to property or substance, changed in kind or appropriated to another use.
From Latin con and verto, to turn — the root also of convert, revert, divert, and version.
scriptures: Matthew 18:3
And said, Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.
Acts 3:19
Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord;
Psalm 51:13
Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee.
Luke 22:32
But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.
corruption_summary: Revivalism replaced conversion with the decision — a countable, engineered response to a technique — and the church now carries millions who were told they were converted because they walked an aisle and cannot remember ever having turned.
corruption_paragraphs: Charles Finney taught explicitly that a revival is not a miracle but the right use of constituted means, and built the anxious bench, the protracted meeting, and the direct appeal for an immediate public decision on that foundation. The machinery outlived the theology and now runs in churches that would repudiate Finney’s Pelagianism. The result is a counting problem that is really a pastoral catastrophe: a man is invited to pray a prayer, is assured on the spot that he is saved, and is then instructed to doubt any later evidence to the contrary. Acts 3:19 puts repentance first and Matthew 18:3 makes conversion the entrance requirement to the kingdom; neither passage authorises anyone to pronounce the verdict on a stranger’s soul at the end of a meeting.

The opposite drift, common where the first error is being corrected, denies that conversion has any datable or perceptible character at all, so that no one may ever be asked whether he has turned. That is not the New Testament either. Paul could recount his turning; the Thessalonians turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9); Peter’s restoration in Luke 22:32 is a specific event with a before and after. The Reformed answer holds both: God alone gives the new heart, and He gives it so that the man actually turns — sometimes with a remembered hour and sometimes without, but always with a changed direction that others can see.
roots_summary: Greek epistrepho (G1994), to turn about, to turn back; strepho (G4762), to turn; metanoia (G3341), a change of mind; Hebrew shub (H7725), to turn back, to return — the great prophetic call word.
roots_lines: Greek epistrepho (G1994) — to turn round, to turn toward; the standard verb of conversion (Acts 3:19, 9:35, 26:18).
Greek strepho (G4762) — to turn; used in Matthew 18:3, where the KJV renders it be converted.
Greek metanoia (G3341) — a change of mind issuing in a change of course; the inward side of the same turning.
Hebrew shub (H7725) — to turn back, return; over a thousand occurrences, the prophets’ constant summons to Israel.
Hebrew teshubah (H8666) — a returning; the noun formed from shub, the Old Testament shape of repentance.
usage: Except ye be converted… ye shall not enter (Matthew 18:3) — the turning made the condition of entrance.
Repent ye therefore, and be converted (Acts 3:19) — repentance and conversion preached together.
When thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren (Luke 22:32) — restoration after a fall, given for the sake of others.

etymology: From Latin purificare, to make pure, from purus (clean, unmixed) and facere (to make). Webster 1828: freed from foreign or heterogeneous matter; cleansed from guilt or the defilement of sin. The metallurgical image — ore purified in the furnace — stands behind most of the biblical usage.
biblical_def: Purified in Scripture describes what God does to the inside of a man, and the New Testament is emphatic that the instrument is faith and the agent the Spirit, never ceremony. Peter reports the Jerusalem council’s decisive argument about the Gentiles: God gave them the Holy Ghost, And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith (Acts 15:9). The heart is the object, faith the means, and the same work in Jew and Gentile alike — which ended the question of circumcising the nations. Peter says the same to the scattered churches: Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently (1 Peter 1:22). Purity is not privacy; its stated end is love of the brethren, and a man who claims a purified soul and hates his brother has disproved his claim. The purchase price was the death of Christ: Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works (Titus 2:14). And the hope of seeing Him works backward into present conduct: every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure (1 John 3:3). Daniel adds the furnace: Many shall be purified, and made white, and tried (Daniel 12:10).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PURIFIED as freed from extraneous matter; cleansed; freed from guilt or the defilement of sin; and, in the ceremonial sense, freed from legal uncleanness by the appointed rites.
webster_full: PURIFIED, pp. — Freed from foreign or heterogeneous matter; cleansed; refined, as metal in the furnace.
Freed from guilt or the defilement of sin; made holy in heart and life.
In the ceremonial sense, cleansed from legal pollution by the rites appointed under the law.
Cleared from improper mixture or corruption; as, a purified language or a purified worship.
From Latin purus, pure, and facio, to make — the root also of pure, purity, and purgatory (the last a corruption of the doctrine, not of the word).
scriptures: Acts 15:9
And put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith.
1 Peter 1:22
Seeing ye have purified your souls in obeying the truth through the Spirit unto unfeigned love of the brethren, see that ye love one another with a pure heart fervently:
Titus 2:14
Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.
1 John 3:3
And every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself, even as he is pure.
Daniel 12:10
Many shall be purified, and made white, and tried; but the wicked shall do wickedly: and none of the wicked shall understand; but the wise shall understand.
corruption_summary: Purgatory takes the word and moves the purifying beyond death into a place of satisfaction the believer must undergo himself, which denies that the blood of Christ purges the conscience once for all.
corruption_paragraphs: The Roman doctrine of purgatory holds that souls dying in grace but with temporal punishment still owing are purified by suffering before entering glory, and that the living may shorten that suffering by indulgences, masses, and almsgiving. The doctrine is built on 2 Maccabees, a book outside the Protestant canon, and on a reading of 1 Corinthians 3:15 that turns a statement about a builder’s work being burned into a statement about the builder being burned. Hebrews 9:14 says the blood of Christ shall purge your conscience from dead works, and Hebrews 10:14 that by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. If one offering perfected them for ever, there is no remainder for a furnace beyond death to consume, and the indulgence traffic that provoked Luther was the practical fruit of the error.

A second corruption is subtler and lives inside evangelical churches: the reduction of purity to sexual behaviour policed by pledges and rings, so that a young person is taught that purity is a status he keeps or forfeits by a single act. Acts 15:9 locates the purifying in the heart and assigns it to faith; 1 Peter 1:22 makes its object love of the brethren. Chastity is commanded and the dictionary does not soften it — but a purity culture that treats virginity as the thing purified has misplaced both the object and the agent, and it leaves the fallen with no gospel, since a status once forfeited cannot be restored by the scheme that defined it.
roots_summary: Greek katharizo (G2511), to cleanse, to purify; hagnizo (G48), to purify ceremonially or morally; katharos (G2513), clean, pure; Hebrew taher (H2891), to be clean; barar (H1305), to purge, to make bright.
roots_lines: Greek katharizo (G2511) — to cleanse, to make clean; purifying their hearts by faith (Acts 15:9).
Greek hagnizo (G48) — to purify, akin to hagios, holy; used of the soul in 1 Peter 1:22 and of self-purifying hope in 1 John 3:3.
Greek katharos (G2513) — clean, unmixed; Blessed are the pure in heart (Matthew 5:8).
Hebrew taher (H2891) — to be clean, to purify; the Levitical word for the cleansed leper and the purged sanctuary.
Hebrew barar (H1305) — to purify, to make bright, to select; behind purified in Daniel 12:10.
usage: Purifying their hearts by faith (Acts 15:9) — the argument that ended the circumcision controversy.
Purify unto himself a peculiar people (Titus 2:14) — the purchase and its purpose.
Every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself (1 John 3:3) — expectation of seeing Christ working backward into conduct.

etymology: From Latin re (again) and novus (new), through the English renew. Webster 1828: made new again; repaired; restored to a former state or to a good state after decay; regenerated. Scripture uses it of strength restored, of the inward man daily repaired, and of the mind remade after the image of the Creator.
biblical_def: Renewed in the New Testament describes a daily work of God on the inward man that runs exactly opposite to what is happening to the body. For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16). Two processes, one man, opposite directions: the outward wasting, the inward repaired — and the wasting is the very cause Paul gives for not fainting. The renewal has a definite object and a definite pattern: And have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him (Colossians 3:10). Knowledge is the sphere, and the pattern is the Creator’s own image, so that sanctification is the restoration of what Adam lost. Ephesians locates the work precisely: And be renewed in the spirit of your mind (Ephesians 4:23) — not the mind considered as intellect only but the governing disposition behind the thinking, which is why Romans 12:2 makes the renewing of the mind the means of proving the will of God. The Old Testament adds the promise to the waiting: they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles (Isaiah 40:31), and the psalmist marvels that God satisfieth thy mouth with good things; so that thy youth is renewed like the eagle’s (Psalm 103:5).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines RENEWED as made new; restored to a former or to a better state; repaired; refreshed; and, in theology, regenerated — renewed in the spirit of the mind by the operation of the Holy Spirit.
webster_full: RENEWED, pp. — Made new again; restored to a former good state after decay, injury, or depravation.
Repeated; begun again; as, a renewed assault or a renewed covenant.
Refreshed; recruited; as, strength renewed by rest or by waiting upon God.
In theology, regenerated; renovated in heart and mind by the Holy Spirit after the image of God.
From Latin re, again, and novus, new — the root also of novel, innovate, and renovation.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 4:16
For which cause we faint not; but though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.
Colossians 3:10
And have put on the new man, which is renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him:
Ephesians 4:23
And be renewed in the spirit of your mind;
Isaiah 40:31
But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.
Psalm 103:5
Who satisfieth thy mouth with good things; so that thy youth is renewed like the eagle's.
corruption_summary: The self-care industry has taken the vocabulary of renewal and detached it from God, so that the renewing of the mind is offered as a technique for restoring the self rather than the Spirit’s restoration of the Creator’s image in a fallen man.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 40:31 is quoted more often on gym walls and coffee mugs than in any other setting, and almost always with its subject removed. The renewing belongs to them that wait upon the LORD; the promise is not that exhausted people recover if they rest but that people who look to God are carried by God. Detached from that clause the verse becomes a motivational slogan, and the slogan fails the first person whose strength does not return — which is precisely the situation Isaiah was addressing, a nation in exile with nothing left. The chapter opens with Comfort ye, comfort ye my people and grounds the comfort in the everlasting God who fainteth not, neither is weary. The strength renewed is His, lent, not the sufferer’s own reserve rediscovered.

The second displacement is therapeutic. Romans 12:2 and Ephesians 4:23 are routinely enlisted for programmes of thought-management in which the renewed mind means an inventory of negative self-talk replaced with affirmations. Colossians 3:10 gives the actual content and pattern: renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him. The knowledge is knowledge of God, the pattern is the imago Dei defaced in Adam, and the agent is the Spirit through the Word. Where the technique is aimed at a better opinion of the self, Scripture aims at a truer knowledge of God and a lower estimate of the self, and 2 Corinthians 4:16 is content to let the outward man perish while that work goes on.
roots_summary: Greek anakainoo (G341), to renew, to make new in quality; anakainosis (G342), renewal; ananeoo (G365), to renew in the spirit of the mind; Hebrew chadash (H2318), to be new, to renew, to repair.
roots_lines: Greek anakainoo (G341) — to make new in quality, not merely new in time; 2 Corinthians 4:16 and Colossians 3:10.
Greek anakainosis (G342) — renewal; the renewing of the Holy Ghost (Titus 3:5) and the renewing of your mind (Romans 12:2).
Greek ananeoo (G365) — to renew, to make young again; only at Ephesians 4:23, of the spirit of the mind.
Hebrew chadash (H2318) — to renew, repair, rebuild; used of repairing the altar and of renewing the kingdom (2 Chronicles 15:8; 1 Samuel 11:14).
Hebrew chalaph (H2498) — to change, to pass on, to renew; behind shall renew their strength in Isaiah 40:31.
usage: The inward man is renewed day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16) — two opposite processes in one man.
Renewed in knowledge after the image of him that created him (Colossians 3:10) — sanctification as restored image.
They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength (Isaiah 40:31) — the promise with its subject kept in place.

etymology: From Latin testificari, to bear witness, from testis (a witness) and facere (to make). Webster 1828: bore witness to; affirmed or declared solemnly; gave evidence. The word is legal before it is religious: a testis is a man in court whose word is evidence.
biblical_def: Testified is courtroom language pressed into the service of the gospel, and the New Testament never treats preaching as opinion offered but as evidence given. Paul at Corinth is described in exactly these terms: Paul was pressed in the spirit, and testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ (Acts 18:5). The content is a fact about a Person, not a philosophy, and Paul is under pressure to state it. The summary of his whole ministry among Jews and Greeks alike is the same word: Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 20:21) — one message, two directions, both parts required. Testimony also runs backward through the prophets, and the Witness is the Spirit of Christ Himself: when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow (1 Peter 1:11). The Old Testament writers were not guessing about a coming figure; the Spirit within them gave evidence in advance. Hebrews can cite a psalm simply as testimony without naming the human author: But one in a certain place testified, saying, What is man, that thou art mindful of him? (Hebrews 2:6). And the ransom itself is spoken of as evidence entered at the appointed hour: Who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time (1 Timothy 2:6).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines TESTIFIED as borne witness to; affirmed or declared solemnly, as under oath; given evidence of; and, in the scriptural sense, declared or made known by divine revelation or by the solemn charge of a prophet.
webster_full: TESTIFIED, pp. — Borne witness to; affirmed or declared solemnly, as in a court of justice.
Given evidence of; manifested; made evident by open declaration or by conduct.
Declared with earnest protestation; charged solemnly, as a prophet testifying against a people.
In the scriptural sense, made known by revelation, as the Spirit testifying beforehand of the sufferings of Christ.
From Latin testis, a witness, and facio, to make — the root also of testimony, attest, protest, and testament.
scriptures: Acts 18:5
And when Silas and Timotheus were come from Macedonia, Paul was pressed in the spirit, and testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ.
Acts 20:21
Testifying both to the Jews, and also to the Greeks, repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ.
1 Peter 1:11
Searching what, or what manner of time the Spirit of Christ which was in them did signify, when it testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ, and the glory that should follow.
Hebrews 2:6
But one in a certain place testified, saying, What is man, that thou art mindful of him? or the son of man, that thou visitest him?
1 Timothy 2:6
Who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time.
corruption_summary: Modern evangelism has largely replaced testimony to Christ with testimony about the self, so that my testimony now means the story of a life rather than evidence given concerning a Person and His work.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 18:5 and Acts 20:21 define the content of apostolic testimony without ambiguity: that Jesus is the Christ, and repentance toward God with faith toward the Lord Jesus. Neither text contains a word about the speaker’s biography. When testimony shifts to mean the narration of one’s own experience, three things follow. The evidence becomes unfalsifiable and therefore unarguable, which is comfortable but useless. The dramatic conversion outranks the quiet one, so that the man saved at seven has nothing to say. And the hearer is left to judge Christianity by the improvement in a stranger’s life rather than by the resurrection of Christ, which is the evidence Paul actually put forward in 1 Corinthians 15.

The second corruption is the therapeutic reframing of witness as the sharing of lived experience, in which the authority of the account rests on the speaker’s having undergone it and is therefore beyond challenge. Scripture does use experience — the man born blind said one thing I know, that, whereas I was blind, now I see — but he said it in defence of a claim about Christ, under interrogation, and he was arguing. The Bible’s witnesses give testimony that can be examined: dates, places, named officials, five hundred brethren at once, most of whom Paul says are still alive. The dictionary keeps the legal sense: a witness is a man whose word is evidence about something outside himself, and the Spirit of Christ testifying beforehand in the prophets (1 Peter 1:11) is the pattern for all Christian witness.
roots_summary: Greek martureo (G3140), to bear witness; diamarturomai (G1263), to testify solemnly, to charge earnestly; marturia (G3141), testimony; martus (G3144), a witness, whence martyr; Hebrew ud (H5749), to testify, to warn.
roots_lines: Greek martureo (G3140) — to bear witness, to give evidence; the ordinary courtroom verb (John 15:27; 1 John 5:9).
Greek diamarturomai (G1263) — to testify thoroughly, to charge solemnly; Paul’s word in Acts 20:21 and 2 Timothy 4:1.
Greek marturia (G3141) — the testimony given; the word of their testimony by which the saints overcome (Revelation 12:11).
Greek martus (G3144) — a witness; the English martyr, because witnesses so often sealed the evidence with blood.
Hebrew ud (H5749) — to bear witness, to warn repeatedly; thou didst testify against them (Nehemiah 9:34).
usage: Testified to the Jews that Jesus was Christ (Acts 18:5) — the content of the evidence given.
Testifying… repentance toward God, and faith toward our Lord Jesus Christ (Acts 20:21) — the whole ministry in one clause.
It testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ (1 Peter 1:11) — prophecy as advance evidence by the Spirit of Christ.

etymology: From Latin magnificare, to make great, from magnus (great) and facere (to make). Webster 1828: made great or greater; enlarged; extolled; praised highly. Of God the sense is never to increase Him but to declare His greatness, as a lens does not enlarge a star but shows it as it is.
biblical_def: Magnified is used of God, of His word, and of His servants, and in each case the greatness declared is real greatness made visible rather than greatness manufactured. God cannot be increased; He can be shown. So the psalmist calls for a verdict to be repeated rather than a quantity added: let them say continually, Let the LORD be magnified, which hath pleasure in the prosperity of his servant (Psalm 35:27). Astonishingly, God magnifies His word above even His name: for thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name (Psalm 138:2) — the written revelation set higher than the reputation, which is the strongest possible statement of the authority of Scripture and comes from God’s own side. At Ephesus the outcome of the failed exorcism is stated in one clause: fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified (Acts 19:17). The city did not add to Christ; it saw Him truly and was afraid. God also magnifies men in office, and the purpose is always the securing of His own work: On that day the LORD magnified Joshua in the sight of all Israel; and they feared him, as they feared Moses (Joshua 4:14). And Paul makes his own body the instrument, indifferent to the manner: Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death (Philippians 1:20).
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines MAGNIFIED as made great or greater; enlarged in bulk or in appearance; extolled; exalted in praise; and, when applied to God, celebrated as great, since no addition can be made to infinite greatness.
webster_full: MAGNIFIED, pp. — Made great or greater; enlarged, as an object viewed through a glass.
Extolled; exalted in representation; praised highly and openly.
Applied to God, celebrated and declared to be great; for the divine greatness admits of no increase.
Raised in the esteem of others; as, the LORD magnified Joshua in the sight of all Israel.
From Latin magnus, great, and facio, to make — the root also of magnitude, magnificent, and magnify.
scriptures: Psalm 35:27
Let them shout for joy, and be glad, that favour my righteous cause: yea, let them say continually, Let the LORD be magnified, which hath pleasure in the prosperity of his servant.
Psalm 138:2
I will worship toward thy holy temple, and praise thy name for thy lovingkindness and for thy truth: for thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name.
Acts 19:17
And this was known to all the Jews and Greeks also dwelling at Ephesus; and fear fell on them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
Philippians 1:20

According to my earnest expectation and my hope, that in nothing I shall be ashamed, but that with all boldness, as always, so now also Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death.
Joshua 4:14
On that day the LORD magnified Joshua in the sight of all Israel; and they feared him, as they feared Moses, all the days of his life.
corruption_summary: Where Scripture magnifies God before men, the modern platform magnifies the man before God’s people, and the celebrity structure of contemporary ministry has made the confusion nearly invisible to those inside it.
corruption_paragraphs: Acts 19:17 is worth reading against any modern account of a successful meeting. Nobody was persuaded by eloquence; seven men were beaten by a demon they had presumed to command with a borrowed formula, fear fell on the whole city, and the outcome was that the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified. The next verses record confession of deeds and the burning of fifty thousand pieces of silver in occult books. That is what it looks like when Christ is magnified in a city: the reputation that grows is His, the cost falls on the people, and the preacher is not mentioned. Where a ministry’s growth consistently magnifies its founder’s name, the pattern of Acts 19 is worth applying without flinching.

Psalm 138:2 is the answer to the other corruption, which sets the living voice above the written word — whether as papal magisterium, as a prophetic word claiming fresh revelation for the church, or as the more genteel version in which the text must yield to what the Spirit is thought to be doing now. God has magnified His word above all His name. That is not a devotional flourish; it is a statement of the order of authority from the mouth of God, and it means that any claimed leading, impression, tradition, or council which contradicts the written word is thereby disproved. The Reformation principle of sola Scriptura is simply this verse taken seriously.
roots_summary: Hebrew gadal (H1431), to be great, to make great, to magnify; gadol (H1419), great; Greek megaluno (G3170), to make great, to magnify; megas (G3173), great.
roots_lines: Hebrew gadal (H1431) — to grow, to be great, to magnify; O magnify the LORD with me (Psalm 34:3).
Hebrew gadol (H1419) — great; the adjective behind the great and dreadful day of the LORD.
Greek megaluno (G3170) — to make great, to enlarge, to extol; My soul doth magnify the Lord (Luke 1:46).
Greek megas (G3173) — great; the root of the English mega- and of megaleiotes, majesty.
Greek doxazo (G1392) — to glorify; the near neighbour of megaluno, both declaring what God already is.
usage: Let the LORD be magnified (Psalm 35:27) — a verdict repeated, not a quantity added.
Thou hast magnified thy word above all thy name (Psalm 138:2) — the written word set highest by God Himself.
Christ shall be magnified in my body, whether it be by life, or by death (Philippians 1:20) — the servant indifferent to the manner.
